dev_facts.fact: Coming from neurorehab, I lean on the clinician and caregiver to do the actual informed-consent conversation at onboarding; we hand them an information sheet but I'll admit we don't yet have a standardized, patient-facing consent screen baked into the app itself.

Our whole population is elderly post-stroke or early-dementia, so many patients genuinely lack full decision capacity, and right now the capacity call is left to the clinician's judgment at sign-up; we haven't formalized a documented capacity-assessment workflow or anything like a re-check when someone declines further.

In practice the caregiver or physiotherapist sets up the patient and schedules the exercises, so the patient isn't always the one driving the decision; we do honour a patient or guardian withdrawing, but there's no built-in 'I don't want to play today' button that the patient can hit themselves and have respected.

We designed for cognitive accessibility with large fonts, voice instructions and a simple UI, and tested it with mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment, but I'll be honest that we haven't specifically handled hearing-impaired users (no captions on the voice prompts) or significant motor impairment, and we haven't run a formal WCAG audit.

We co-designed with two memory clinics and tested with real patients, which I'm proud of, but it was light-touch usability work rather than structured iterative UCD rounds, and we haven't deliberately checked whether older users find the game framing condescending or confusing.

Our evidence is one pilot RCT of N=80 against paper exercises with a small but significant improvement; the clinician review currently just shows progress and 'improvement', and I'll concede we don't surface effect sizes, confidence intervals or the caveat that an N=80 result may not generalize.

We target Swiss and German nursing homes and home-care, so device, connectivity and the cost of who pays for the tablet are real barriers for poorer home-care patients; we haven't really thought through socioeconomic access beyond assuming the care facility provides the hardware.
The app is in German for the DACH/CH market, but I have to admit we built one German variant and haven't validated CH-German versus AT/DE idioms or task wording with local clinicians in each region.

We've assessed ourselves as a Class IIa software medical device under MDR Rule 11 because we drive therapy decisions for a clinical condition, and since there's no AI in the product we've taken the view that the AI Act classification doesn't apply to us.

CE marking under MDR is in progress but not finished yet, so we're not fully MDR-conformant at this moment; our post-market plan so far is an annual safety review with our clinical advisory board rather than a formalized continuous vigilance system.
